```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(cowplot)
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

bd <- read.csv("../../data/Focal_Bird_Morphology.csv")
bd <- bd[bd$species %in% c("jawe", "rwbu", "wrsh") &
             !is.na(bd$nares_to_tip), ]

n <- min(table(bd$species))

set.seed(123)
bd <- lapply(split(bd, bd$species), \(x) {
    x[sample(nrow(x), n), ]
})
bd <- do.call(rbind, bd)

bd$full_name <- "Japanese white-eye"
bd$full_name[bd$species == "rwbu"] <- "red-whiskered bulbul"
bd$full_name[bd$species == "wrsh"] <- "white-rumped shama"
```

# How do we describe \alert{data}?

## How do we describe \alert{data}?

- Why do we make the choices we make in describing data?
- These choices get bundled into knowledge system
- Whose knowledge system(s) do we learn and why?


## Learning Objectives

1. Describe the *location* of numerical variables using the \alert{mean} and \alert{median}
2. Describe the *spread* of numerical variables using the \alert{standard deviation}, \alert{variance}, \alert{coefficient of variation}, and \alert{interquartile range}
3. Describe categorical variables using the \alert{proportion}
4. Know when to use different descriptive statistics

## Describing location and spread of numerical data

**the Mean describes location**


\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{l l l p{4cm}}
Descriptor & Parameter & Estimate & Units \\
\hline
mean & $\mu$ & $\bar{Y}$ & measurement unit (e.g. cm, seconds, etc.)    
\end{tabular}
\end{center}



Notes:

- $\mu$ is Greek letter pronounced like "mew"
- $\bar{Y}$ pronounced like "Y bar"

## \alert{Sample mean}


In words:

> The \alert{sample mean} is the sum of all the observations in a sample divided by $n$, the number of observations

In math:

$$\bar{Y} = \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^{n} Y_i}{n}$$

## \alert{Sample mean}

```{r}
wrsh <- bd$nares_to_tip[bd$species == "wrsh" & !is.na(bd$nares_to_tip)]
```

## Describing location and spread of numerical data

**the Standard Deviation describes spread**


\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{l l l p{4cm}}
Descriptor & Parameter & Estimate & Units \\
\hline
mean & $\mu$ & $\bar{Y}$ & measurement unit \\
standard deviation & $\sigma$ & $s$ & measurement unit 
\end{tabular}
\end{center}


Notes:

- $\sigma$ ("sig-ma") is Greek letter "s"


## \alert{Sample standard deviation}

In words:

> The \alert{standard deviation} is a common measure of the spread of data. It indicates how far the different measurements are (on average) from the mean.

In math:

$$
\begin{aligned}
s^2 &= \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^{n} (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2}{n - 1} \\
s &= \sqrt{s^2}
\end{aligned}
$$

$s^2$ is the sample variance

Take square root to get standard deviation: $\sqrt{s^2} = s$


## \alert{Sample standard deviation}

**FAQ**

Q1: Why does the sum of squared deviations ($\sum_{i = 1}^{n} (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2$) appear in the numerator?

A1: Negative and positive deviations have the same effect on average deviation. For example, suppose $\bar{Y} = 0$:

$$(1 - 0) ^ 2 = (1) ^ 2 = 1$$
$$(-1 - 0) ^ 2 = (-1) ^ 2 = 1$$

## \alert{Sample standard deviation}

**FAQ**

Q2: Why use the sum of squared deviations rather than absolute deviations?

A2: The squared values turn out to have better statistical properties than absolute values.

## \alert{Sample standard deviation}

**FAQ**

Q3: Why is it divided by $n-1$ rather than $n$?

A3: Dividing by $n$ is \alert{biased} and *underestimates* the population standard deviation. Matters most when $n$ is small.

## \alert{Sample standard deviation}

```{r}
m <- round(mean(wrsh[1:8]), 2)
```

Remember: $\bar{Y} =$ `r m` mm

```{r}
data.frame(c(as.character(1:8), "**Sum**"), 
           c(wrsh[1:8], sum(wrsh[1:8])), 
           c(paste(wrsh[1], "-", round(mean(wrsh[1:8]), 2), "=", 
                   round(wrsh[1] - round(mean(wrsh[1:8]), 2), 2)), 
             rep("", 8))) |> 
    kable(col.names = c("$i$", "$Y_i$", "Deviations ($Y_i - \\bar{Y}$)"))
```


## \alert{Sample standard deviation}

By definition, sum of deviations equals 0

```{r}
s <- data.frame(c(as.character(1:8), "**Sum**"), 
           c(wrsh[1:8], sum(wrsh[1:8])), 
           c(round(wrsh[1:8] - m, 2), 0)) 

kable(s, col.names = c("$i$", "$Y_i$", "Deviations ($Y_i - \\bar{Y}$)"))
```



## \alert{Sample standard deviation}

Sum of squared deviations is always positive

```{r}
s <- cbind(s, "")
s[1, 4] <- paste0("$(", s[1, 3], ")^2$ = ", round(s[1, 3]^2, 4))

kable(s, col.names = c("$i$", "$Y_i$", "Deviations ($Y_i - \\bar{Y}$)", 
                       "Squared deviations $(Y_i - \\bar{Y})^2$"))
```

## \alert{Sample standard deviation}

Sum of squared deviations is always positive

```{r}
s[, 4] <- round(s[, 3]^2, 4)
s[9, 4] <- round(sum(s[1:8, 4]), 4)

kable(s, col.names = c("$i$", "$Y_i$", "Deviations ($Y_i - \\bar{Y}$)", 
                       "Squared deviations $(Y_i - \\bar{Y})^2$"))
```

## \alert{Sample standard deviation}

$$s^2 = \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^{n} (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2}{n - 1} = \frac{`r s[9, 4]`}{7} = `r round(s[9, 4]/7, 4)`~\mathrm{mm}^2$$
```{r}
wrsh_s <- round(sqrt(round(s[9, 4]/7, 4)), 4)
```

$$s = \sqrt{`r round(s[9, 4]/7, 4)`} = `r wrsh_s`~\mathrm{mm}$$

The standard deviation has the same units as the measurements (mm in this case), so you can describe the departure from the mean in a consistent way.

"Almost 95% of data typically fall within two standard deviations of the mean"

## Describing location and spread of numerical data

**Coefficient of Variation is standard deviation as a percentage of the mean**

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{l l l p{4cm}}
Descriptor & Parameter & Estimate & Units \\
\hline
mean & $\mu$ & $\bar{Y}$ & measurement unit \\
standard deviation & $\sigma$ & $s$ & measurement unit \\
variance & $\sigma^2$ & $s$ & measurement unit$^2$ \\
coefficient of variation & $\sigma/\mu \times 100\%$ & CV & percent (\%)
\end{tabular}
\end{center}


Notes:

- CV is useful for comparing data with different measurement units


## \alert{Coefficient of variation}

In words:

> The \alert{coefficient of variation} is the standard deviation expressed as a percentage of the mean

In math:

$$\mathrm{CV} = \frac{s}{\bar{Y}} \times 100\%$$

## \alert{Coefficient of variation}

$$\mathrm{CV} = \frac{s}{\bar{Y}} \times 100\% = \frac{`r wrsh_s`}{`r m`} \times 100\% = `r round(wrsh_s / m * 100, 2)` \%$$

## Describing location and spread of numerical data

- Rank species by mean beak length by eye
- Rank species by standard deviation beak length by eye

```{r}
bd |>
  group_by(full_name) |>
  summarize_at(vars(nares_to_tip), list(m = mean, s = sd)) |>
  mutate(CV = paste0(round(100 * s / m, 2), "%")) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Species", "$\\bar{Y}$", "$s$", "CV"), 
        digits = c(0, 2, 2, 0))
```

Note: statistics for larger data set (not subset of 8)

The mean and the spread increase together. This is common for morphological data.

## Describing location and spread of numerical data

 Descriptor | Parameter | Estimate | Units 
------------|-----------|----------|-------
 median     | Median    | $M$      | measurement unit

Notes:
 
- "\alert{median} is the middle observation in a set of data"

## \alert{Median}

If $n$ is *odd*:

$$\text{Median} = Y_{([n+1]/2)}$$
If $n$ is *even*:

$$\text{Median} = [Y_{(n/2)} + Y_{(n/2+1)}]/2$$

## Median

```{r}

X <- data.frame(wrsh = sort(wrsh[1:8]), 
                label = sort(wrsh[1:8]), i = 1:8)

gp <- ggplot(X, aes(x = i, y = 0, label = label)) +
    geom_text(vjust = -0.5, size = 6) +
    geom_path(data = data.frame(i = range(X$i) + c(-0.5, 0.5), 
                                y = 0, label = NA),
              color = "tomato", size = 2) +
  annotate("line", x = rep(nrow(X) / 2 + 0.5, 2), y = c(3, 1),
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.5, "cm")), color = "tomato", size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = nrow(X) / 2 + 0.5, y = 3, vjust = -0.5,
           label = "Median", size = 12) +
  ylim(0, 4) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void() 

gp

# Data frame to ensure calculations below are correct and easily portable
df = rename(X, Y = wrsh) |>
  arrange(Y)
Y = df$Y
n = nrow(df)
```

$$n = `r nrow(X)`$$

$$\text{Median} = \frac{Y_4 + Y_5}{2} = \frac{`r Y[n/2]` + `r Y[n/2+1]`}{2} = `r sprintf("%.2f", round(median(Y), 2))`~\text{mm}$$

## Describing location and spread of numerical data

 Descriptor | Parameter | Estimate | Units 
------------|-----------|----------|-------
 median     | Median    | $M$      | measurement unit
 interquartile range | Interquartile range    | $IQR$      | measurement unit

Notes:
 
- "\alert{\textit{IQR}} is the difference between the third and first quartiles of the data. It is the span of the middle 50\% of the data."

## Interquartile range

```{r, warning=FALSE,message=FALSE}

gp + 
  annotate("line", x = rep(nrow(X) / 4 + 0.5, 2), y = c(3, 1),
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.5, "cm")), color = "tomato", size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = nrow(X) / 4 + 0.5, y = 3, vjust = -0.1,
           label = "First\nquartile", size = 12) +
  ylim(0, 5)

```

$$j = 0.25 n = 0.25 \times `r n` = `r ceiling(0.25 * n)`$$

$$\text{First quartile} = \frac{Y_`r ceiling(n / 4)` + Y_`r ceiling(n / 4) + 1`}{2} = \frac{`r Y[ceiling(n / 4)]` + `r Y[ceiling(n / 4)+1]`}{2} = `r sprintf("%.2f", round( (Y[ceiling(n / 4)] + Y[ceiling(n / 4)+1]) / 2, 2))`~\text{mm}$$

## Interquartile range

```{r, warning=FALSE,message=FALSE}

gp + 
  annotate("line", x = rep(nrow(X) / 4 + 0.5, 2), y = c(3, 1),
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.5, "cm")), color = "tomato", size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = nrow(X) / 4 + 0.5, y = 3, vjust = -0.1,
           label = "First\nquartile", size = 12) +
  annotate("line", x = rep(nrow(X) * 0.75 + 0.5, 2), y = c(3, 1),
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.5, "cm")), color = "tomato", size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = nrow(X) * 0.75 + 0.5, y = 3, vjust = -0.1,
           label = "Third\nquartile", size = 12) +
  ylim(0, 5)

```

$$k = 0.75 n = 0.75 \times `r n` = `r ceiling(0.75 * n)`$$

$$\text{Third quartile} = \frac{Y_{`r ceiling(n * 0.75)`} + Y_{`r ceiling(n * 0.75) + 1`}}{2} = \frac{`r Y[ceiling(n * 0.75)]` + `r Y[ceiling(n * 0.75)+1]`}{2} = `r sprintf("%.2f", round( (Y[ceiling(n * 0.75)] + Y[ceiling(n * 0.75)+1]) / 2, 2))`~\text{mm}$$

## Interquartile range

```{r}
first_quartile  = (Y[ceiling(n * 0.25)] + Y[ceiling(n * 0.25)+1]) / 2
third_quartile  = (Y[ceiling(n * 0.75)] + Y[ceiling(n * 0.75)+1]) / 2
```


$$\text{Interquartile range} = \text{Third quartile} - \text{First quartile} = `r sprintf("%.2f", round(third_quartile - first_quartile, 2))`~\text{mm}$$

$$\mathit{IQR} = `r sprintf("%.2f", round(third_quartile, 2))` - `r sprintf("%.2f", round(first_quartile, 2))` = `r sprintf("%.2f", round(third_quartile - first_quartile, 2))`~\text{mm}$$

## 3. Describe categorical variables using the \alert{proportion}

 Descriptor | Parameter | Estimate | Units 
------------|-----------|----------|-------
 proportion     | proportion    | $\hat{p}$      | probability

Notes:

- the \alert{sample proportion} is similar to the \alert{sample mean}


## \alert{Sample proportion}

In words:

> The \alert{sample proportion} is a measure of the **location** of categorical data. It indicates how frequently a specific category is found in the data.

In math:

$$
\hat{p} = \frac{N_{[Y = \text{category}]}}{n}
$$

## 4. Know when to use different descriptive statistics

When data are roughly symmetrical and there are not many extreme values

- mean, standard deviation, variance are commonly used
- CV if you want to compare values on different scales

When data are skewed and/or there are many extreme values

- median tells more about a typical unit in the population and is less sensitive to extreme values
- IQR is less sensitive to extreme values than standard deviation


## Rounding

* No standard rules
* For this class, round to 2 decimal places
